hero_title: From one page to eight, and what that cost.
hero_deck: How this portfolio became a multi-page site — and what the commit record shows about both builds.
hero_rv_txt: I refused to stop at the slide. I learned front-end development, then rebuilt the result as eight pages under a written scope.
act1_verdict: The page was not the problem. What it could not separate was.
act1_scan1: One page held everything. Every visitor got the same scroll.
act1_scan2: Eight pages let each case be found on its own — and made the architecture the work.
act2_lede: Four stops, from designing pictures of software to building it.
act2_verdict: I learned to build — then made building answer to a standard I wrote down.
act2_s1_x: I designed for years in Canva, Figma, and Framer while builders like Webflow, Wix, and WordPress stayed someone else's system.
act2_s2_x: I chose to learn front-end development itself, not coding in the abstract, with a Microsoft specialization laying the foundations.
act2_s3_x: The first portfolio wasn't a portfolio. It was jdigital.pe, a brand site — re-pointed once I knew what I actually had to show.
act2_s4_x: Eight pages replaced the scroll. Each case got its own route, and the architecture became part of what the work shows.
act3_verdict: The evidence is public — and you're standing in it.
act3_lede: This is not a case about a product I once touched. The evidence is the site itself: live, versioned, and open to inspection. Four claims, each one checkable.
act3_c1_x: Every section of this site is built from reusable components under one standard — so nothing drifts, and new pages inherit quality instead of reinventing it.
act3_c1_rv_txt1: Ten reusable organisms — navigation, hero, work cards, capability carousel, timeline, contact, and footer among them — each held to correct adoption of the global token layer. The structure beneath is semantic: header, nav, main, section, and footer landmarks, a single top-level heading, and a clean hierarchy below it, so browsers, assistive technologies, and other developers read the same order a visitor sees.
act3_c1_rv_txt2: Design rules are declared once at the root as custom properties and referenced everywhere — change a token, and the change propagates. Layout runs on Flexbox and Grid with one consistent type scale. All interface copy is dictionary-driven, so a new language enters as a data file, not a rewrite.
act3_c2_x: Nothing to patch, nothing to migrate, nothing borrowed — no rented platform, no stack of dependencies rotting quietly while you're not looking.
act3_c2_rv_txt: Hand-authored HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with no framework I couldn't justify, and no build tooling. Every style rule lives in one external system — no inline patches, no exceptions — which is what keeps the standard enforceable. No third-party dependencies means no forced migrations, no security-patch treadmill, and a payload small enough to stay fast without optimization theater.
act3_c3_x: Usable with screen readers and keyboards, held to a recognized international standard from the first line of code — a requirement, not a repair.
act3_c3_rv_txt: WCAG AA held as a build gate: every meaningful image described in alt text, every form control paired with its label, landmarks distinguished with aria labels, visible focus styles so keyboard users always know where they are, and text contrast held at the 4.5:1 floor. Accessibility claims sit on this very page — which means they can be tested against it.
act3_c4_x: Speed came from AI; the standard stayed with me. Every build session runs under written rules and approval gates before anything ships.
act3_c4_rv_txt1: Structured XML dispatches govern every build session — scope, constraints, and approval gates written before execution. Claude Code executes with Plan Mode previews reviewed before code lands; deployment follows hard rules with named commit intent — register, direct push, or a pull request with its link for manual approval — and authorship is logged to a single human author.
act3_c4_rv_txt2: And when a stubborn spacing defect in the site's contact form outlasted the primary environment, a second AI tool, Gemini, rebuilt the component cleanly from zero for reintegration into the master codebase — the right tool, invoked when needed, under the same standard.
act4_verdict: Running today, governed daily, by me alone.
act4_insight: The number that matters is the ratio: nothing I ship lands without passing a gate I set for myself. The page you're reading is the evidence.
dash_r1: The signal isn't the volume. It's the ratio. 286 commits mean momentum; 49 pull requests mean restraint. A review gate roughly every six commits is the cadence design organizations try to install in whole teams — I run it on myself.
dash_r2: Beneath the numbers sits a qualitative floor: the build meets a graded professional rubric for semantic structure, accessibility, styling discipline, interactivity, and responsive behavior.
dash_r3: What transfers to your team isn't my code. It's this operating habit.
dash_foot: Method: public GitHub history, 24 Apr – 06 Jul 2026 (73 days). Rates are simple averages — 286÷73, 49÷10.4, 286÷49. Figures verifiable at the repository linked above.
act5_verdict: What fell, what bent, what stands.
act5_intro: The story reads clean in hindsight. It wasn't. Here is the journey in three houses, in the order I built them.
act5_h1_x: My first prompts were plain text and good intentions. They decayed as builds grew, I chased every flag to closure, and template shortcuts gave me speed without ownership. It blew down — and falling taught me exactly what a foundation is for.
act5_h2_x: Iteration cycles ate whole sessions. One bug outlasted my main environment and needed a second tool. My documentation lived scattered across chats before a system existed. The structure held, barely — and every bend showed me where the next wall belonged.
act5_h3_x: Versioned dispatches with approval gates. Skills that turn my intent into build-grade prompts. Project knowledge as the order I had historically lacked. Previews before code lands. And the habit of letting best judgment close the small flags — instead of overthinking them.
act5_sequel: The sequel is already dispatched: per-case pages, the Spanish layer, and the next product rebuild. The houses get neighbors.
convert_c1_x: A media-accreditation platform with a full UX dossier and 545 tests behind it.
convert_c2_x: A payment-verification flow rebuilt as an operator-legible sequence.
sch_verdict: Seventy-three days on the first build. Seventeen on the second.
sch_lede: Each epic below is reconstructed from the public commit history of both single-page repositories. Planned-capacity days appear here and nowhere else on this page.
sch_note: Reconstructed from the public commit history of github.com/jdsaire/jdigital and github.com/jdsaire/legacy-desops, summed across both — 24 Apr – 06 Jul 2026. 32 active build-days; three further dates in June carried document uploads rather than site code and are excluded. The closing Ground Zero reorganization (06 Jul, ~1 day) is my own account, not a commit. No task appears that the record cannot support.
gantt_seq_text: Sequence: the jdigital repository ran first, then legacy-desops, then designops. This is the order the three repositories were worked in, not a chain of blocking dependencies.
gantt_noscript: This component renders from its data object and requires JavaScript. Every window it draws is also stated in the note below.
gantt_caption_body: Bars are calendar spans, not effort. A gap is a real gap: nothing was committed on those days. Each row carries an information button naming that row's window and where it came from. The dotted row is my own account rather than a commit. The record ends on 06 September 2026 and nothing is drawn past it — four further stages are dispatched and carry no date to draw: this one, the Spanish layer, the repository README and the closing audit.
